title: Looking Closely at a Snowflake
description: Explore a snow crystal through its branches, symmetry, and the clouds in which it forms.
cardDescription: Explore a snow crystal through its branches, symmetry, and the clouds in which it forms.
focus: Many snow crystals have sixfold symmetry, although their detailed shapes vary with formation conditions.
solvingTip: Start with the ordinary shape words before the longer crystal terms.

answerNotes.SNOWFLAKE: A falling snowflake can be a single crystal or several joined crystals.
answerNotes.CRYSTAL: The internal structure of ice helps produce its characteristic sixfold forms.
answerNotes.HEXAGON: Hexagonal plates are one possible form of snow crystal.
answerNotes.BRANCH: Branches grow as water vapor joins the crystal under suitable conditions.
answerNotes.SYMMETRY: Real snow crystals can be irregular even when the underlying structure is symmetrical.

title: Sleet, Snow, and Freezing Rain
description: Compare familiar winter precipitation words through the form water takes before and after reaching a surface.
cardDescription: Compare familiar winter precipitation words through the form water takes before and after reaching a surface.
focus: In U.S. weather usage, sleet is ice pellets; freezing rain falls as liquid and freezes on contact with cold surfaces.
solvingTip: Use the described form of the precipitation to choose each answer.
words: Small ice pellets falling from the sky in U.S. weather usage
Smooth ice coating left when freezing rain freezes on contact
Small rounded piece of ice in sleet
Precipitation made of very small liquid drops
Wet mixture of snow and liquid water
Precipitation falling as ice crystals or joined flakes
Liquid drops falling from a cloud
Become solid as a water drop turns to ice
Warm enough to let frozen precipitation melt
Single small portion of liquid precipitation
Cover a branch with a layer of ice
Travel surface that may become icy in a storm
Describing a surface covered with liquid water
Low in temperature, as a freezing surface is

answerNotes.SLEET: Sleet differs from freezing rain because its drops freeze before reaching the ground.
answerNotes.GLAZE: Glaze is an ice deposit, rather than the falling liquid itself.
answerNotes.PELLET: An ice pellet has already frozen while still in the air.
answerNotes.DRIZZLE: Drizzle describes drop size; freezing drizzle can form ice on cold surfaces.
answerNotes.SLUSH: Slush is a mixture on the ground rather than one distinct falling crystal.

title: Shorter Days and Low Winter Sun
description: Follow daylight, shadows, and the seasons through the ordinary words used to describe the winter Sun.
cardDescription: Follow daylight, shadows, and the seasons through the ordinary words used to describe the winter Sun.
subtheme: Shorter Days and Low Winter Sun
focus: Earth's axial tilt changes seasonal daylight; winter is not caused simply by Earth being farther from the Sun.
solvingTip: Distinguish a time of day from the light or shadow seen then.
words: Seasonal point associated with the shortest Northern Hemisphere day
Slant of Earth's axis responsible for the seasons

answerNotes.SOLSTICE: The December solstice marks the shortest daylight period in the Northern Hemisphere.
answerNotes.TILT: Earth's axis stays tilted as the planet travels around the Sun.
answerNotes.DAYLIGHT: Daylight duration varies with both season and latitude.
answerNotes.SHADOW: A low Sun often creates a longer shadow than a high Sun.
answerNotes.HORIZON: Sunrise and sunset are observed near the horizon.

title: Wind Chill on a Winter Morning
description: Compare air temperature, wind, and the familiar words used to describe a colder-feeling winter day.
cardDescription: Compare air temperature, wind, and the familiar words used to describe a colder-feeling winter day.
subtheme: Wind Chill on a Winter Morning
focus: Wind chill estimates heat loss from exposed skin under specified conditions; it does not lower the measured air temperature.
solvingTip: Distinguish measured temperature from the effect of moving air.

answerNotes.WINDCHILL: Wind chill represents an effect on heat loss rather than a second air temperature.
answerNotes.THERMOMETER: Wind chill does not change the temperature measured by a properly placed thermometer.
answerNotes.EXPOSED: The wind-chill concept concerns heat loss from exposed skin.
answerNotes.GUST: A gust differs from the sustained or average wind speed.
answerNotes.HEAT: Wind can increase heat transfer away from a warm surface.

answerNotes.SNOWPLOW: A snowplow clears by moving snow, rather than melting it with heat.
answerNotes.BLADE: The blade is the working attachment at the front of many plow trucks.
answerNotes.SPREADER: A spreader distributes material behind or beneath the vehicle.
answerNotes.WINDROW: Windrow can also describe rows of cut hay in another setting.
answerNotes.GRIT: Grit provides friction and is different from a salt deicer.
